# The Four Prayoga Sub-Stages

## Warming, Peak, Patience, and the Best the World Can Do

Anyone who has learned a physical skill knows this sequence, even if nobody named it for them.

First something starts to work. Not reliably, not on demand, but occasionally the thing happens and you can feel that it happened. **Warming.**

Then it gets good. You have a best day, and on that day you can do it. You cannot repeat it tomorrow. **The peak.**

Then comes the long ugly stretch where the peak will not come back and you keep going anyway. Nothing improves for months. This is where most people quit, and the name for the stage is exactly right: **patience**, or forbearance.

And then a plateau that is genuinely high — the best you can do while still doing it the way you have been doing it. **Highest worldly attainment.** The ceiling of the ordinary approach.

Buddhism uses these four to partition the second stage of the path, the stage of intensified preparatory practice. The Sanskrit collective term is the *nirvedha-bhāgīya*, the portions conducive to penetration. Bodri lays them out at page sixteen and returns to them for eight pages afterwards.[^1]

## They Are Not His

This page exists partly to correct a record, and the correction matters more than it might appear.

The vault already held these four, at second hand, through an intermediary corpus, where they were labelled **"Bodri's four stages."** Both pages carrying them hedged the attribution and flagged that it rested on a targeted reading of a secondary document.

The primary text settles it. He presents them as **Buddhism's own** partition of the preparatory stage — *"Buddhism does exactly this, and partitions the Stage of Intensified Practices into a sequence of four phases"* — and then matches them to the *Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā*'s four-fold scheme of *ārambha*, *ghaṭa*, *paricaya* and *niṣpatti*, calling that "almost an exact matching of teachings."[^1]

So the hedging pointed at the wrong risk. **The danger was never that the attribution was too weak. It was that calling them "Bodri's" over-credits the transmitter.** He is a conduit here, and says so.

That is a small correction with a large moral, and it is treated at [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/identical-metaphor-different-attainment|Identical Metaphor, Different Attainment]]: what dropped out of the chain of transmission was not a citation. It was a **doctrinal-tradition marker** — a Buddhist scheme of the path of preparation, arriving somewhere else in devotional clothing, with nothing in the vocabulary to signal that it had moved.

## The Recursive Claim

The four are more interesting than a stage-list because Bodri says they do not apply once.

They apply to **every** gong-fu. To **every** absorption, individually. So a practitioner working on the second dhyāna goes through warming, peak, patience and highest-ordinary inside that one attainment, and then does it again in the third.

And then the claim that makes the page worth building: they apply to **learning to cook, to ice-skate, to ride a bike.**[^2]

That is Bodri drawing the cross-domain connection himself, which is rarer and more valuable than a vault-imposed one. The scheme is not a description of spiritual progress that happens to resemble skill acquisition. On his account it *is* skill acquisition, running at every scale, and the contemplative case is one instance rather than the parent.

If that is right, then the four are not a doctrine to accept but a shape to check — and everyone reading has already lived through it several times, in domains where the evidence is public.

## What "Highest Worldly Attainment" Is Actually Saying

The fourth name repays a second look, because it is doing something the other three are not.

The first three describe how the practitioner feels. The fourth describes a **limit**. *Laukikāgradharma* — the highest of worldly dharmas — is the best result available inside the ordinary frame, and the point of naming it is that going further is not a matter of doing more of the same.

That is why the whole four-part sequence sits inside the *preparatory* stage rather than spanning the path. You can execute all four perfectly and be exactly where the stage-scheme says: prepared. The plateau at the top of them is not a failure of effort. It is what completed effort looks like from inside, and the thing that follows it is a different kind of event.

This is the structural point most likely to be lost when the four get borrowed, because a four-stage sequence naturally reads as *a path*, and readers supply a fifth stage where the tradition supplies a discontinuity.

## Implementation Workflow

You have been working at something for two years and it has gone flat.

You had a period early on where it started working. You had a stretch, maybe six months in, where you were noticeably good — and you have not been that good since. Now it is grinding and you are wondering whether you have the aptitude, or whether this was the wrong thing to spend two years on.

Locate yourself before deciding anything.

**Ask whether the peak actually happened.** Not whether it was sustained — whether there was a period, however short, when the thing worked. If yes, the capacity is established and the current flatness is not evidence against it. If no, you may genuinely still be in warming, and warming can take much longer than anyone tells you.

**Then ask how long the flat stretch has run.** This is the stage the scheme names *patience*, and naming it is most of the help. The flatness is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is the stage, and it is the one that eliminates people — not because they lack the capacity but because nothing in the experience distinguishes "grinding through the necessary stretch" from "wasting my time."

**Then check what you are still doing the same.** If you have been flat for a long time and everything about the approach is unchanged, you may be at the fourth stage rather than the third — the ceiling of the current method. Those two feel identical from inside and need opposite responses: patience means keep going, ceiling means change something structural.

**And expect to run the sequence again.** Bodri's recursive claim is the practically useful part. The next capacity you build will have its own warming, its own peak, its own long flat stretch. Knowing that in advance does not make the flat stretch shorter. It stops you reading it as a verdict.

## Analytical Case Study: The Same Four in a Yoga Manual

The strongest thing Bodri does with these four is not the exposition — it is the cross-check, and it is worth examining because it is one of the few correspondences in the book that survives his own criterion.

He sets the Buddhist four beside the *Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā*'s: **ārambha** (the beginning, when the practice starts to take), **ghaṭa** (the vessel, when things consolidate), **paricaya** (accumulation, the long gathering), **niṣpatti** (completion, the final ordinary perfection).

Two things make this a better match than most of the book's correspondences.

**The schemes are structurally parallel rather than lexically similar.** He is not matching a word for warmth to a word for warmth. He is matching four positions in two four-part sequences that both describe the same stretch of the same kind of work — the consolidation phase before something else has to happen. The names do not resemble each other at all, which is a point in favour rather than against.

**And the fourth terms agree about the *limit*.** *Niṣpatti* means completion, and in the yogic scheme it is the perfection of the preparatory work, not of the path. *Laukikāgradharma* is the highest of worldly dharmas. Both traditions independently place a **named ceiling** at the end of four stages, and both treat what comes after as discontinuous.

That is agreement on a structural feature rather than on imagery, and it is the kind of match [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/buddhism-as-comparative-reference-grid|Buddhism as a Comparative Reference Grid]] argues is the only reliable sort. Whether the two traditions are describing the same terrain remains unproven. But they are at least making the same *shape* of claim, and the shape is checkable.

## Why Four, and Why These Four

The collective name is the most informative thing about the set, and Bodri does not use it — the *nirvedha-bhāgīya*, the portions **conducive to penetration.**

That framing tells you what the four are for. They are not four qualities to develop, and not four experiences to have. They are the segments of a run-up. Each is named for what is happening to the practitioner's relationship with the material rather than for a state achieved: heat is friction beginning, a peak is the highest point of a curve, patience is what is required when the curve flattens, and the fourth is the top of the ordinary range.

Read that way the sequence is not arbitrary, and you can see why it resists being extended. Add a fifth and you would have to name something between "the best the ordinary approach produces" and the discontinuity — and there is nothing there. Remove one and the account loses either the early flicker or the flat stretch, which are the two segments practitioners most need named, for opposite reasons: the first because it is easy to over-read, the second because it is easy to quit inside.

## What Happens After the Ceiling

The scheme's most important feature is the thing it does not describe, and it is worth stating because a reader will otherwise supply it.

After the fourth stage there is no fifth stage of the same kind. The four are the whole of the preparatory sequence, and what follows them is not more of it.

That is why the tradition treats the transition as a break rather than a step — and why Bodri's larger frame puts *Seeing the Tao* in a different category from the stage that precedes it rather than at the top of the same ladder. The four take you to the edge of what refining an approach can produce. They do not, on this account, produce the thing on the other side, and nothing about executing them well makes the crossing more likely except by removing obstructions to it.

This is the part most easily lost in transmission. A four-part sequence has a strong natural reading as *a path to somewhere*, and every borrowing of these four that this build has traced reads them that way. The tradition's own reading is narrower and stranger: **a run-up whose completion is not an arrival.**

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**Strongest support.** The four are attested in Bodri with those glosses, presented as Buddhism's own partition rather than his invention, and cross-checked against a named yogic scheme with a parallel structure. The recursive extension to ordinary skills is the source's own, which removes the usual worry that the vault has imposed a secular reading.

**The tension the source does not close.** If the four apply to learning to cycle as well as to the second dhyāna, then either the contemplative case is not special, or the four are so general that locating yourself among them tells you very little. Bodri wants both — a universal shape *and* a specific diagnostic — and does not say how a scheme that fits everything constrains anything.

**A second tension, inherited.** These sit inside the preparatory stage, which is the stage the book relocates nearly all world practice into. So the four are simultaneously the most portable thing in the book and a description of the part of the path Bodri says almost nobody gets past. Both are true and they read very differently depending on which you meet first.

**And the standing status line.** The stage-apparatus these four sit inside is disclaimed by its own author — see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/false-stages-and-the-footnote-that-says-so|False Stages, and the Footnote That Says So]]. The four are offered as a rest stop and a morale aid, not as a measurement.

**Open questions.** Does the yogic four-fold scheme mark the same discontinuity after *niṣpatti* that the Buddhist one marks after highest-worldly-attainment — or is the parallel only in the first three? And if the sequence recurs at every scale, what determines the grain at which you should be locating yourself?

## Author Tensions & Convergences

The direct correction runs to [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-bhumi-kanda-correspondence-system|The Bhūmi-Kāṇḍa Correspondence System]], which carries these four at second hand under the wrong attribution. That page's hedge should be replaced rather than removed: the content it reported was accurate, and the framing over-credited the transmitter. The deeper finding is that a Buddhist preparatory scheme travelled into a devotional corpus and arrived re-badged, which is a case study in exactly the transmission failure the source itself describes.

Against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/dharana-dhyana-samadhi-samyama|Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, Samādhi, Saṃyama]], the relationship is one of scale rather than rivalry. Patañjali's sequence describes the deepening of concentration; the four *prayoga* stages describe the consolidation of *any* practice, including that one. On Bodri's recursive claim they should nest — each of Patañjali's stages having its own warming, peak, patience and ceiling — and that is a specific prediction the vault could check against the *Yoga Sūtras* directly.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**The stage that eliminates people** — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/ego-development-theory-hub|Ego Development Theory Hub]]. The third term is the one worth taking outside the tradition. *Patience* names the long unrewarding stretch after early progress stops and before consolidation shows, and its defining property is that **nothing inside the experience distinguishes it from failure**. The developmental literature has the same problem under other names — plateau, arrest, the long middle — and the same practical difficulty: the person in it cannot tell, from inside, whether persistence is warranted. **The insight the pairing produces: the flat stretch is not a signal that can be read, and treating it as one is the error** — which means the decision to continue has to be made on grounds other than how the work currently feels, and any framework that promises to tell you which flat stretch you are in is overselling.

**Ceilings that are not failures** — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/decline-mechanisms-hub|Decline Mechanisms Hub]]. The fourth term names something most progress models lack: a **completed** limit, where the approach has been executed properly and has reached the end of what it can produce. Institutions hit this constantly and almost never diagnose it correctly, because the symptoms of a method at its ceiling and a method being executed badly are identical — flat results, no obvious error, effort undiminished. **Neither side gives this alone: distinguishing a ceiling from a plateau requires evidence from outside the method, and a method at its ceiling is precisely a method that has stopped generating such evidence** — which is why the diagnosis is almost always made late, and usually by someone who arrived from elsewhere.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** **The fourth stage is a ceiling, not a summit — and a four-part sequence naturally reads as a path, so readers reliably supply a fifth stage where the tradition supplies a discontinuity.** That misreading is most of what goes wrong when this scheme travels.

**Generative questions.**
- If the sequence recurs at every scale, what fixes the grain at which a practitioner should locate themselves — and is a person ever in only one instance of it at a time?
- Patience and ceiling feel identical from inside and require opposite responses. Is there any internal marker that separates them, or is external evidence strictly necessary?
- The scheme fits contemplative practice and bicycle-riding equally well. Does that generality make it a finding or a truism?

# Vayu: The Ambiguous Wind-God

## The God Who Stands in the Doorway

Every other god in this system picks a side — Light or Dark, good yazata or evil daēva. Vayu, the wind-god, refuses. He stands in the doorway between the two worlds, belonging fully to neither. His own self-description, given to Zarathuštra: "My name is Vayu, because I go through the two worlds, the one which the Good Spirit has made and the one which the Evil Spirit has made."[^1] He passes through both. Both Ahura Mazda *and* Angra Mainyu offer him sacrifice — the only god both sides court.[^2]

He's the wind, and the wind is exactly that: the thing that fills the empty space between earth and sky, between the solid and the void, moving freely where nothing else can. A god of the in-between, with the air of neutrality about him.[^3]

> **Source trust note.** From Billinge's *War Yoga: Zurxāne* (Sanctus Europa Press, an identitarian publisher). Vayu's ambiguity is from the Rām Yašt (Yašt 15); calibrated against Boyce and the Vedic Vāyú comparison. The männerbund/wolf-warrior framing is handled descriptively; the source's identitarian glorification is excluded.

## What This Actually Is

Vayu (Vedic **Vāyú**) is the god of the wind and of the warrior-band.[^4] His name means "Wind" — one of the two key elements of the hero (along with fire).[^5] He's "first to receive sacrifice among the war gods," marking his importance to war, and the Rām Yašt says he "wears the raiment of warfare."[^6]

His defining trait is **ambiguity**. Vayu "straddles the material realm and Otherworld... traverses and fills the void between opposites."[^7] He has "traits of both Light and Dark" and "straddles the line between daēva and good yazata."[^8] This isn't fence-sitting — it's a *function*. The wind is what operates in the void between the stone vault of heaven (Asman) and the earth; that void "is where Vāta and Vayu operate."[^9]

The ambiguity has two faces, sharply:
- As **destroyer**, "he severs the soul from the body" — the death-wind that cuts the cord.[^10]
- As **guide**, "he transports the souls of the dead to the Činvat Bridge where they are judged."[^11]

So the *same* god both kills you (severs soul from body) and guides you (carries the soul to judgement). He's the psychopomp who is also the reaper — death and the escort through death in one figure.

The Avesta also splits him: **Vāta** is the physical wind (elemental force, tied to Mithra and Vərəθragna), while **Vayu** is the metaphysical Wind, always a distinct personality.[^12] Later Pahlavi thought doubles him again into *vāy ī weh* (good wind) and *vāy ī badtar* (evil wind) — the ambiguity formalised into two winds.[^13]

## Why the In-Between Is a Power

Here's the thing the tradition understands that most moral systems miss: the figure who *moves between* the opposites has a power the figures locked into one side don't. Vayu can go where Mithra (committed to Light) and Ahriman (committed to Dark) cannot — into the other's territory, through the void, across the line. The wind isn't compromised by its neutrality; it's *enabled* by it.

This is why Vayu is the psychopomp. Guiding a soul *across* the boundary between life and death, world and Otherworld, requires a god who himself lives in the crossing — who isn't fully on either shore. A purely good god couldn't enter death's territory; a purely evil one couldn't be trusted to deliver the soul to judgement. Only the in-between god can carry you across. His ambiguity is his qualification.

And it's the trait the warrior aims to emulate: "This is a trait the young wolf warrior aims to emulate" — the capacity to traverse and fill the void between opposites.[^14] The fighter who can move between states — controlled and ferocious, present and detached — has the wind's freedom that the locked-in fighter lacks. (The source's excluded framing romanticises the "wolf warrior" and the *furor*; the disciplined reading keeps the structural insight — mobility between states as power — and drops the berserker glorification.)

## What This Page Gives the Vault

Vayu is the **liminality/psychopomp** node of [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/mithra-attendant-yazatas|Mithra's warband]]. He's [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/verethragna-victory-god|Vərəθragna's]] first avatar (the Victorious Wind). He's the god given prominence in [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/zurvan-time-and-fate|Zurvānism]] (Vay wears the warrior's red, fights Ahriman directly in the final battle). And he feeds the [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/celestial-mountain-hara-barazaiti|Činvat Bridge]] (he carries souls there). For the Indic limb he connects to [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/five-vayus-bodily-winds|the five vāyus]] — the bodily winds — and to Hanumān (the Vāyu-son).

## Analytical Case Study: The Reaper Who Is Also the Guide

The strangest and most instructive thing about Vayu is that the *same* god severs the soul from the body (kills you) and carries the soul to judgement (guides you). Most traditions split these — a reaper and a psychopomp, a killer and an escort. Iran fused them into one ambiguous wind.[^15]

Sit with what that means. The force that ends your life is the *same* force that conducts you onward. Death and the journey through death aren't two separate agents; they're one wind with two faces. The cut and the carrying are the same gesture seen from either side. This is a far more unified and unsettling picture than a reaper handing you off to a guide — it says the thing that takes you apart is the thing that moves you on, that severance *is* transport.

The practical reading, carried inward: every real transition in a life works this way. The force that *ends* a stage of you — that severs you from who you were — is the same force that *carries* you to the next. The job-loss that cuts you from your old identity is the wind that moves you toward the new one; the same gust does both. We tend to experience the severance (destroyer-Vayu) and the guidance (psychopomp-Vayu) as opposite forces, one cruel and one kind. Vayu says they're one wind. Which means: don't wait for the kind guide to arrive *after* the cruel reaper. The reaper *is* the guide. The thing cutting you loose is already carrying you across.

## Implementation Workflow: Moving With the Wind, Not Against It

You're in a transition that feels like pure loss — something is being severed, and you're braced against it, treating the cut as the enemy and waiting for relief to come later. That's resisting Vayu, fighting the wind.

Instead you do the in-between move. You recognise that the force severing you from the old state is the *same* force that will carry you to the new one — destroyer and guide are one wind. So you stop bracing against the cut and let it move you. You don't cling to the shore you're being taken from; you let the wind that's cutting you loose also carry you. Concretely: when something ends and you feel the severance, you ask "where is this carrying me?" instead of "how do I stop the cut?" — because it's the same wind, and the carrying only becomes available once you stop fighting the cut.

And the warrior-version: you practise *mobility between states*. When you're locked rigid in one mode — all aggression, or all control, or all grief — you deliberately let the wind move you across, into the complementary state, the way Vayu passes between worlds. The power isn't in holding one state; it's in being able to traverse them. You become the wind in the doorway, not the figure nailed to one room.

## The Failure Mode: Ambiguity as Excuse, or Rigidity as Safety

Vayu fails in two opposite ways. First, **ambiguity as moral evasion**: using the in-between to avoid ever taking a side, mistaking Vayu's *functional* neutrality (the wind that crosses to do a job) for "nothing matters, I commit to nothing." But Vayu, for all his ambiguity, "always fights on the side of Light and Aša" when it counts — he's "still a moral force compared with his Vedic counterpart."[^16] His crossing is in service of the good (he delivers souls to *judgement*, not into the dark). Ambiguity-as-function is not ambiguity-as-cowardice.

Second, the opposite failure — **rigidity as safety**: refusing the wind entirely, locking into one state because crossing feels like death. The diagnostic sign is a person who can only operate in one mode and treats every transition as pure threat, never letting the severing-wind carry them anywhere. They survive the cut but never reach the far shore, because they wouldn't let the reaper-who-is-also-the-guide do its second half.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

Vayu's ambiguity and his destroyer/guide duality are from the Rām Yašt, well-attested.[^17] The Vāta/Vayu (physical/metaphysical wind) distinction and the later good-wind/bad-wind doubling are textual. The live tension: the source notes Vayu "may have been above Indara in an earlier strata" — that the wind-god may once have outranked Indra before the Vedic Indra's rise.[^18] This reconstruction of an earlier wind-supreme layer is inferential. Held as such.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Billinge follows the standard reading (Boyce, the Vedic Vāyú comparison) on Vayu's ambiguity and psychopomp role. His distinctive emphasis is the *warrior-emulation* reading — Vayu's between-worlds mobility as the model for the "wolf warrior." The careful scholarly reading keeps Vayu primarily as a *cosmological* ambiguous deity (the wind in the void, the death-wind) rather than a martial ideal to imitate. Read together, the tension is whether Vayu's liminality is a *feature of the cosmos* or a *capacity to cultivate*. The convergence (the destroyer-guide duality, the in-between function) is textual; the "warrior emulates the wind's mobility" is the practitioner overlay — useful as a psychological reading, but the source's version drags it toward the excluded *furor*-glorification, which the vault strips out while keeping the mobility-between-states insight.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

Plainly: a force that both ends a state and carries you to the next — and a power that comes from *moving between* opposites rather than holding one — maps onto the psychology of transition and the skill of range.

- **Psychology:** [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/shadow-integration|Shadow Integration]] — Vayu-as-destroyer-who-is-also-guide is a precise image of how real transformation works: the force that *severs* you from an old identity is the same force that *carries* you to the new one, and treating them as separate (waiting for the kind guide after the cruel cut) stalls the crossing. The parallel produces a usable reframe for any painful transition: the severance and the transport are one wind, so the question is never "how do I stop the cut" but "where is this carrying me" — and the carrying only opens once you stop bracing against the cut.
- **Behavioral-mechanics:** [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/authority-and-composure|Authority and Composure]] — Vayu's between-worlds mobility is the operator's *state-range*: the capacity to move fluidly between modes (controlled/ferocious, warm/cold, present/detached) rather than being locked in one. The insight neither generates alone: power often belongs to the figure who can *cross* between states, not the one committed to a single register — the locked-in operator is predictable and trappable, while the one who moves like the wind between modes can go where the committed one can't. Mobility itself is the advantage.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication.** If the force that severs you from who you were is the *same* force that carries you to who you're becoming, then every transition you've experienced as "first the loss, then maybe later the new thing" was actually one continuous wind that you split in two by bracing against the cut. The reaper and the guide are one. Which means the relief you're waiting for *after* the severance is already present *in* it — you just can't feel the carrying while you're fighting the cut.

**Generative Questions**
- Vayu fuses the reaper and the psychopomp into one wind. What changes in how you handle loss if you genuinely believe the thing ending you is the thing moving you on — rather than waiting for a separate rescue?
- The wind's *neutrality* is what lets it cross where committed gods can't. Where is functional neutrality a power (the negotiator, the psychopomp, the translator) versus where is it cowardice — and what distinguishes Vayu's crossing-to-serve from mere fence-sitting?
- Iran *split* the wind into physical (Vāta) and metaphysical (Vayu), then doubled Vayu into good and evil winds. Why does the wind specifically keep getting subdivided — is the in-between always under pressure to be sorted into sides?

## Connected Concepts
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/mithra-attendant-yazatas|Mithra's Retinue]] — the warband Vayu belongs to as the liminal psychopomp
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/verethragna-victory-god|Vərəθragna]] — whose first avatar, the Victorious Wind, is Vayu
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/zurvan-time-and-fate|Zurvān]] — where Vay (red, warrior) fights Ahriman in the final battle
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/celestial-mountain-hara-barazaiti|The Celestial Mountain]] — Vayu carries souls to the Činvat Bridge here
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/five-vayus-bodily-winds|The Five Vāyus]] — the Indic bodily-wind cousins

# Foreknowledge Across the Military Corpus

## The Chorus That Never Stops Singing

Here is a parlor trick you can play with two thousand years of Chinese military writing. Open any of the major texts to its passage on war and intelligence, cover the title, and read it aloud. The Ssu-ma Fa, parts of which may predate Sun-tzu: "employ spies against the distant; observe the near."[^1] Wu Ch'i, a generation or so after: among the four vital points of warfare, "affairs" means "being good at controlling clandestine operatives."[^2] Sun Pin, Sun-tzu's brilliant descendant: among five paths to victory, "one who analyzes the enemy and estimates the terrain will be victorious"; among five paths to defeat, "one who does not use spies will not be victorious."[^3] The Huai-nan Tzu, Li Ching of the T'ang, the Sung *Unorthodox Strategies*, an unnamed Ming author — cover the titles and you cannot tell them apart. They are all singing the same note: *know first, then move.*

That is the whole argument of this page. The insistence on foreknowledge was not Sun-tzu's private obsession or a quirk of one famous chapter. It was the spine of the entire corpus, repeated by author after author, dynasty after dynasty, for the better part of two thousand years — a chorus so unbroken that the individual voices blur into one continuous demand.[^4]

## What This Actually Is

This concept is the *consensus* — the documented fact that virtually every serious Chinese military writer, across every dynasty Sawyer surveys, independently insisted that intelligence and advance knowledge must precede the commitment of armies. It is not a single doctrine but a convergence of many, and the convergence is itself the point.

Sawyer states the throughline plainly: "Because of the analytical nature of their approach to warfighting, virtually all the Chinese military writers addressed the need for an intelligence service to ferret out vital information unavailable from open sources and simple observation."[^5] The texts agree on the verb — *know* — and on its position in the sequence — *first*. They disagree only on emphasis and idiom: one stresses terrain, another stresses the enemy's government, another the enemy's general, another the enemy's troops. But the demand to know before acting is constant.

The chorus also agrees that agents are not passive collectors. Wu Ch'i's spies actively sow dissension, "forcing rulers and ministers to feel mutual annoyance, higher and lower ranks to reproach each other."[^6] Sawyer reads this directly: "such agents did not just passively gather information, but also actively engaged in sowing dissension and undermining administrations."[^7] So the foreknowledge the corpus demands is not only the kind you read off — it is the kind you create by reaching into the enemy and stirring.

## How a Chorus Becomes Proof

The mechanism worth understanding is *why repetition across independent voices matters more than any single brilliant statement.* One genius saying "know your enemy" is a slogan. Twelve unrelated authors across two thousand years independently building their war theory on the same axiom is structural evidence — it tells you the principle was not idiosyncratic but foundational to how an entire civilization reasoned about war.

Listen to how the same note recurs in different keys. The *Kuan-tzu*: trying to undertake military affairs while ignorant of estimations is "like wanting to cross over a dangerous river without a boat or oars."[^8] Li Ching of the T'ang: decisive victory lies in "investigating the opposing general's talent and abilities; analyzing the enemy's strengths and weaknesses... first being victorious, only thereafter engaging in combat."[^9] The Sung *Unorthodox Strategies*: "first employ spies to determine the enemy's troop strength... and only thereafter mobilize the army."[^10] Three texts, three dynasties, one sequence — spies first, mobilization second. The Ming author is the most violent about it: a general who confronts the enemy "but does not know the enemy's situation is a blockhead," and one who skips spycraft "is a wild animal."[^11]

The recurrence does something a single voice cannot. It converts "Sun-tzu believed X" into "the tradition was built on X." And it sets up the page's payoff: when a Western historian points to Sun-tzu's lone "advance knowledge must be gained from men" passage and treats it as the whole story, the chorus is the rebuttal. The principle was everywhere, which means no single text owns it — and which also means, as the corpus itself admits, the principle's universality did not stop the prognosticatory tradition from flourishing right beside it.[^12]

## What This Gives the Rest of the Vault

This page is the *consensus backstop* for every intelligence concept in the vault. When another page makes a claim about Chinese intelligence doctrine, this page is the evidence that the claim is not built on Sun-tzu alone — that the principle had a dozen independent witnesses. It is the page you cite when you need to say "this was the tradition, not one man's opinion."

To [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/chinese-military-theory-historical-development|Chinese Military Theory's Historical Development]] the gift is a *measured constant.* The development page tracks change over time; this page supplies the one thing that did *not* change — the foreknowledge axiom held steady from the Ssu-ma Fa to the Ming while almost everything else around it evolved. A development narrative needs both its variables and its constants, and the demand to know first is the corpus's most durable constant.

To [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/sun-tzu-intelligence-five-spies|Sun-tzu's Five Categories of Spies]] the handshake is *de-centering.* Sun-tzu's chapter is the most famous statement of foreknowledge, but this page shows it was one voice in a chorus, not the source of the song. That reframing protects the vault from the Western error of treating Sun-tzu as a lone prophet — the five spies are the most systematic expression of a demand that the Ssu-ma Fa already made before Sun-tzu wrote.

## Case Study: The Tiger and Its Teeth

The Ming author gives the corpus its sharpest parable, and it deserves a slow walk because it carries the foreknowledge argument past mere "gather information" into something closer to a theory of leverage.[^13]

A tiger eats men. The author runs through the ways a man might deal with it directly, and every one ends the same way. Go to pull out its teeth yourself — you end up eaten. Try to tame it by feeding it meat with your own hand — eaten. Pursue it wielding a halberd — eaten. Pelt it with stones in the open — eaten.[^14] Four direct approaches, four corpses. Confrontation with the dangerous thing, on its own terms, kills you.

Then the inversion: "you should have *other people* pull its teeth, not pull its teeth yourself; entrust *other men* to feed it with meat... have *other men* pursue the tiger with a halberd... Conceal yourself when attacking a tiger with stones, and have other men confront its anger."[^15] The tiger is the enemy state. The "other men" are its own ruler, its own ministers, its own allies — the people you turn against it. The Ming author makes the allegory explicit: this is how you "attack others through their ruler, plot against men through their ministers, disperse their alliances, and instigate conflict among them."[^16]

Here is why this is a *foreknowledge* parable and not just an indirection parable. The author closes with the hinge: "But without agents, how can you investigate their true nature, without spies how can you employ these techniques?"[^17] Every move in the tiger strategy — knowing which minister can be turned, which ally can be split, where the ruler is vulnerable — requires intelligence first. The whole elegant scheme of having others pull the teeth is *impossible without foreknowledge.* Indirection is the goal; spying is the precondition. The parable smuggles the corpus's core demand inside a memorable image: you can only manipulate the tiger through others if your spies have first told you which others to use.

And the Ming author adds the symmetry that makes the demand non-optional: the enemy "also seeks information," plotting against you exactly as you plot against him. To gather nothing and "recklessly engage in battle is senseless."[^18] In a contest where both sides are reaching for the tiger's mind, the side that does not know first is the side that gets eaten.

## Inhabiting the Demand

You command the Three Armies. The enemy is across the valley and your officers want to fight.

You make yourself run the chorus in your head before you answer them, because you were raised on these texts. *Without a boat or oars,* says the Kuan-tzu — and you do not yet have the boat. *First be victorious, only thereafter engage,* says Li Ching — and you have not yet won anything in the counting. You feel the pull of your officers' impatience and you recognize it as the thing every text in your library warned you against.

So instead of giving the order to advance, you give a different order. You send for your agents. Not to fight the tiger — to find out where its teeth are loose. Which of the enemy's ministers resents his ruler? Which ally was paid late and might be split off? You will not pull the teeth yourself. You will spend the next days learning which other men can be made to pull them.

Your officers chafe. The delay feels like cowardice to them. But you have read the parable, and you know which men in the story end up eaten — the bold ones who went straight at the tiger. You hold the army where it is and you wait for the foreknowledge that turns a fight you might lose into a manipulation you cannot lose. *Plans that precede affairs flourish.* You let the plans precede.

## When Foreknowledge Is Faked (Diagnostic Signs)

The first failure is the **blockhead's confidence** — the Ming author's word — the commander who confronts the enemy without knowing his situation and calls it boldness. The diagnostic sign is an army moving on impressions, the order to advance given before the agents have reported. Courage substituting for knowledge is the corpus's named pathology.

The second is **pulling the tiger's teeth yourself.** The sign is direct confrontation where indirection was available — attacking the enemy head-on when his ruler, his ministers, or his alliances could have done the work. The man who insists on facing the tiger personally has refused the foreknowledge that would have shown him the loose teeth, and he ends up in the tiger's mouth.

The third is the **one-sided plot** — remembering that you scheme against the enemy while forgetting that the enemy schemes against you. The sign is intelligence effort spent entirely on offense, none on counterintelligence, in a contest the corpus says is always mutual. To know the enemy while ignoring that he is knowing you is to be half-blind in a fight where both sides reach for the same advantage.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

The evidence here is the breadth of the chorus, and Sawyer assembles it deliberately to make a point against a specific error. Western historians, he says, unfamiliar with the vast corpus, have seized on Sun-tzu's lone passage — "advance knowledge cannot be gained from ghosts and spirits... but must be gained from men" — to conclude that Chinese intelligence theory was founded upon and "strictly limited to human effort."[^19] The chorus complicates this twice over. First, it shows the foreknowledge demand was corpus-wide, not Sun-tzu's alone — so the Western fixation on one passage misreads the structure. Second, and this is the deeper tension, Sawyer immediately undercuts the tidy "purely rational" picture: "even though virtually all the tactical works stress human effort and deny the value of divination... the prognosticatory tradition that originated in the Shang dynasty not only continued to flourish, but also vigorously evolved."[^20]

So the chorus is real but it was never a monopoly. The same civilization that produced twelve texts insisting on human foreknowledge produced "numerous volumes devoted to arcane practices" — interpreting sounds, clouds, weather, the phases of the moon, the numerology of dates.[^21] The military theorists sang "know from men, not ghosts," and the diviners kept reading the clouds right alongside them. The corpus's unanimity on foreknowledge did not extend to unanimity on *what counts as knowledge.*

A tension Sawyer's own method invites: he is braiding texts across two thousand years and a dozen genres into a single chorus, and the smoothness of the chorus is partly his arrangement. The Ssu-ma Fa, Wu Ch'i, Sun Pin, Li Ching, and the Ming author wrote in radically different contexts. Calling them one voice is an interpretive choice — defensible, because they do converge on the demand, but a choice that flattens the distance between a possibly-pre-Sun-tzu ritual-war text and a sixteenth-century treatise. The convergence is genuine; the seamlessness is Sawyer's.

Open question: did the chorus describe practice or prescribe an ideal? Sawyer elsewhere notes rulers "frequently to little avail" ignored exactly this counsel. A principle repeated by every theorist and obeyed by few rulers might be evidence of consensus among writers and *dissensus* between writers and practitioners — the corpus agreeing loudly about something the men in power kept ignoring.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Sawyer's organizing instinct is to show continuity, and the foreknowledge chorus is his strongest case for it — genuinely independent texts, separated by centuries, landing on the same axiom. Where his continuity claim earns the most scrutiny is the dating at the edges. He says parts of the Ssu-ma Fa "may predate" Sun-tzu and that Sun Pin's *Military Methods* was "recently rediscovered after being lost for two thousand years."[^22] Both qualifications matter. If the Ssu-ma Fa predates Sun-tzu, then foreknowledge was a demand Sun-tzu *inherited*, not founded — which strengthens the chorus argument. But "may predate" is doing real work, and the rediscovery of Sun Pin means part of the chorus was silent for two millennia and only recently restored to the score. The continuity Sawyer hears is partly reconstructed from texts that were themselves lost and found.

The richest convergence Sawyer documents is across the boundary the corpus itself drew. The military writers insisted foreknowledge comes from men, not spirits — and yet the same culture's divination tradition flourished beside them. Sawyer does not resolve this; he names it as a standing feature of the record. The honest reading is that "Chinese intelligence theory" was never one thing. It was a loud rationalist chorus and a persistent prognosticatory undertone, sharing a civilization and frequently the same temple, neither silencing the other. The Western historians erred not by hearing the chorus but by mistaking it for the whole music.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**To [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/chinese-military-theory-historical-development|Chinese Military Theory's Historical Development]].** The development page is a story of change; this page is the test of whether the change was deep or cosmetic. Lay them together and a real methodological question surfaces: if every text from the Ssu-ma Fa to the Ming repeats the same foreknowledge demand, was Chinese military theory *developing* across those two thousand years, or merely *re-decorating* a fixed core? The insight neither page generates alone is that continuity and development are not opposites here — the foreknowledge axiom held constant precisely so that everything else (the spy taxonomies, the counterintelligence techniques, the metaphysical framings) could vary around it. The constant is what made the variation legible as a tradition rather than a heap of unrelated manuals. A development narrative without this constant has no spine; this page supplies the spine the development page's variations hang from. And it sharpens a caution: Sawyer's "continuity" may sometimes be the constant axiom masking genuine discontinuity in everything else.

**To [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/sun-tzu-intelligence-five-spies|Sun-tzu's Five Categories of Spies]].** The five-spies doctrine is the corpus's most systematic statement of foreknowledge; this page is the proof that the systematization sat inside a much wider consensus. Reading them together corrects a distortion that neither page fixes alone: the Western tendency to treat Sun-tzu as the lone fountainhead of Chinese intelligence thought. The tiger parable, written perhaps two thousand years after Sun-tzu, makes the same demand — agents first, then everything else — without needing to cite him, because by then the demand was simply the air the tradition breathed. The insight: Sun-tzu's five spies are best understood not as the *origin* of the foreknowledge principle but as its most rigorous *formalization* of a principle the Ssu-ma Fa may already have voiced before him. Treating the five spies as fountainhead inflates one text; treating them as formalization-within-a-chorus restores the actual structure — and that structure only appears when you hold the single most systematic statement beside the documented breadth of the whole.

**To [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/temple-calculation-and-net-assessment|Temple Calculation and Net Assessment]].** Foreknowledge is the input; the temple count is the machine that consumes it. The chorus says "know first"; net assessment says "and here is the worksheet your knowing fills." Together they reveal that the corpus's foreknowledge demand was not vague exhortation but a concrete logistical requirement — every column of the temple tally is a piece of foreknowledge the chorus insists you acquire before the rods come out. Neither page alone shows that "know first" and "count before you march" are the same instruction at two altitudes.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** The Western misreading is instructive beyond China. Historians grabbed Sun-tzu's one quotable line and built a whole thesis on it, missing that the line was a single voice in a two-thousand-year chorus. The lesson is about how traditions get flattened in transmission: a foreign reader finds the most translatable passage and mistakes it for the load-bearing one. The chorus is invisible until you read the untranslated bulk — and most readers never do.

**Generative questions.**
1. If foreknowledge was a demand Sun-tzu inherited from the possibly-older Ssu-ma Fa rather than founded, how much of "Sun-tzu's genius" is actually the genius of a tradition he formalized — and does it matter?
2. The chorus sang "know from men, not ghosts" while the divination tradition flourished beside it. Were these rival camps, or did the same commanders consult both — net assessment for the odds, the turtle shell for the nerve?
3. The tiger parable says only fools pull the teeth themselves. In a contest where both sides know this, who pulls anyone's teeth at all — or does universal indirection collapse into stalemate until someone's foreknowledge is simply better?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/chinese-military-theory-historical-development|Chinese Military Theory's Historical Development]] — the arc across which this constant held; the spine the development hangs from.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/sun-tzu-intelligence-five-spies|Sun-tzu's Five Categories of Spies]] — the most systematic voice in the chorus, not its sole source.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/temple-calculation-and-net-assessment|Temple Calculation and Net Assessment]] — the worksheet foreknowledge fills; "know first" and "count first" are one instruction; this page's sibling.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/economic-argument-for-spies|The Economic Argument for Spies]] — why the foreknowledge the chorus demands is worth funding; this page's sibling.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/divination-and-its-rejection|Divination and Its Rejection]] — the rival tradition that flourished beside the chorus despite the corpus's "from men, not ghosts" insistence.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/estrangement-techniques|Estrangement Techniques]] — Wu Ch'i's spies sowing dissension; foreknowledge that is created, not just collected.

# Keluskar — The Strategic Elevation of Jijabai

## The Unanswerable Card: A Biographer Reaches for the Mother

Picture a writer at his desk in 1907, building the case for a king. K.A. Keluskar wants to do something delicate. He wants to take the two brahmin mentors out of the story — Dadaji Konddev, the steward who supposedly raised the boy, and Ramdas, the saint who supposedly gave him his mission — and he wants to do it without starting a fight. Other historians have already planted their flags. Rajwade says the dream of swaraj came from Dadaji. Ranade says the religious ground was laid by the Pandharpur bhakti movement. To push back directly is to pick a brawl with the brahmin establishment over who owns Shivaji.[^1]

So Keluskar reaches for the one card no one at the table can trump. He plays the mother.

He writes that Jijabai was "the primary influence" of Shivaji's youth.[^2] He says the boy did not even meet Ramdas until 1672, long after the great victories were already won — so the saint could not have lit the fire.[^3] He calls Rajwade's Dadaji theory a "heresy."[^4] And then he lands the line that does the real work: "How true it is that one sweet and loving word from the lips of a mother makes a deeper impression on the heart than ten-thousand speeches."[^5]

That sentence looks like sentiment. It is a move on a board. Laine sees it cleanly: Keluskar "strategically elevates Jijabai here, for what Hindu would ever challenge his ode to the mother?"[^6] The mother is unattackable. To honor her is the safest thing a Hindu writer can do. And in the act of honoring her, Keluskar quietly empties the brahmin mentors of their importance. Nobody can object — because objecting means standing against the mother. That is the whole trick. Praise that demotes. A tribute that is also a demolition.

## What This Actually Is

The strategic elevation of Jijabai is a rhetorical maneuver: you crown an unchallengeable figure as the true source of a hero's greatness, and in doing so you displace the figures you actually want to remove — without ever having to attack them head-on.

Keluskar's target is the brahmin claim on Shivaji. In the standard tellings, two brahmins shape the king. Dadaji Konddev, the administrator, plants the seed of independent rule. Ramdas, the saint, supplies the spiritual charter. Both readings hand the credit for Shivaji's vision to brahmins.[^7] Keluskar wants that credit somewhere else. But he cannot simply say "the brahmins did nothing" — that is a partisan claim, and it invites a partisan war.

So he routes the demotion through the mother. He does not argue that Dadaji was unimportant in the abstract. He argues that the real impulse came from Jijabai, and the brahmin's role shrinks to nothing as a side effect. The mother is the lever. She is chosen precisely because she is beyond dispute. No Hindu reader in 1907 is going to stand up and say a mother's love matters less than a steward's tutoring. The cultural reflex protects the move. Keluskar borrows that reflex and points it at his rivals.[^8]

This is why the elevation is "strategic" rather than merely affectionate. Jijabai may well have been a real and decisive force in Shivaji's life — that is not the point. The point is the *use* Keluskar makes of her. He selects her for the job because of what she cannot be attacked for being. The feeling is genuine; the deployment is calculated. Both things hold.

And the same logic — whose figure gets crowned, whose gets dropped — runs all the way through how the legend is cast. The mother is one instance. The martyrs are another. Which heroes get sung in the long retelling is, just as much, a function of who is doing the singing and what caste they belong to.

## Praise That Demotes (The Internal Logic)

The machinery has three moving parts.

First, the unchallengeable move. Keluskar needs a piece on the board that the other side cannot capture. The mother is that piece. In the Hindu emotional grammar of the period, the mother sits beyond argument — to honor her is reflexive, to question her place is to mark yourself as cold. By making Jijabai the source, Keluskar puts his real claim behind a shield no opponent can lower without looking like a monster.[^9]

Second, the demotion that rides along. Once the mother is the source, the mentors have nowhere left to stand. If Jijabai planted the dream of swaraj, then Dadaji did not — and Keluskar goes further, saying Dadaji actually "laboured hard to counteract" those thoughts.[^10] If the fire was lit in youth by the mother, then Ramdas, met only in 1672 after the victories, arrives too late to matter; Keluskar even cites the historian Sardesai to suggest the influence ran the other way, from king to saint.[^11] The brahmin mentors are not refuted. They are simply crowded out by a figure no one can move.

Third, the caste politics underneath. This is not abstract reverence — it is a positioning play, and the positions are caste positions. Keluskar was a Saraswat, a caste that claimed brahmin status but was ranked beneath the Chitpavan and Deshastha brahmins, and that carried significant alliances with the CKPs.[^12] Saraswats, like CKPs and Marathas, had had their own caste status challenged by the elite brahmins of Maharashtra.[^13] Ranade and Tilak — the men whose readings Keluskar pushes against — were both Chitpavans.[^14] So when Keluskar cuts Dadaji and Ramdas down to size, he is a marginal-brahmin reformer trimming the Chitpavan-brahmin claim on the national hero. The ode to the mother is the polite surface of a caste fight.

The same machinery decides which martyrs the legend remembers. The hero's mother is one piece on the board; the hero's dead are another. And the dead are sung selectively, by whoever has an interest in singing them.

## Synergies & Handshakes: The Saraswat's Whole Hand

Keluskar's elevation of Jijabai is not a stray gesture — it is one card in a coordinated hand, and the rest of the hand confirms the read.

Look at the title of his book: *Ksatriyakulavatamsa Chatrapati Sivajimaharaj yance Caritra* — "The Biography of Chatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, Ornament of the Kshatriya Race."[^15] That word, *kshatriya*, is doing political work before the first chapter. Keluskar presented the biography to the Kolhapur prince Shahu just two years after Shahu had won a long campaign to have his kshatriya status upheld by an authoritative Shankaracharya.[^16] The book opens by reciting Shivaji's descent from the Solar and Lunar dynasties and the Rajput royalty of Udaipur.[^17] A Saraswat author is handing a freshly-vindicated Maratha prince a biography that loudly affirms exactly the kshatriya status the brahmin establishment had been contesting. The genealogy and the mother-elevation are the same project from two angles: both lift the Maratha claim and lower the brahmin gatekeeper.

The handshake with Phule's movement is explicit. Keluskar was Phule's colleague.[^18] His sympathies, Laine notes, run toward the Marathas, the CKPs, and even Phule's entire nonbrahmin movement — and that is exactly what you would expect from a Saraswat whose own caste status had been challenged by the same elite brahmins.[^19] The rejection of the Pandharpur movement's influence — Ranade's central thesis — is the other half of the same handshake. By denying that bhakti reform either shaped Shivaji's vision or did much to ease caste inequality, Keluskar opposes Ranade directly while keeping his own nonbrahmin sympathies intact.[^20] Every move points the same way.

## Analytical Case Study: One Sweet Word, and Two CKP Martyrs

Take the sentence itself. "The glorious thoughts of founding a new Hindu dynasty were not implanted in Shivaji's mind by Dadaji Kondadev, who on the other hand laboured hard to counteract them.... The real impulse then came from Jijabai. How true it is that one sweet and loving word from the lips of a mother makes a deeper impression on the heart than ten-thousand speeches."[^21]

Read it as argument and it is thin — there is no evidence offered that Jijabai said any particular word, or that Dadaji counteracted anything. Read it as a move and it is masterful. The first clause demotes the brahmin steward (he not only failed to inspire, he actively worked against the dream). The second clause installs the mother. The third clause — the "sweet and loving word" — makes the installation unanswerable, because to dispute it you would have to argue that a mother's love is weaker than a tutor's lessons, and no Hindu reader of 1907 will take that side. The sentimental flourish is not decoration. It is the lock on the door.[^22]

Now watch the same caste-logic select the martyrs. Phule, and his colleague Keluskar, both lavish attention on two heroes who happen to be CKPs. The first is Baji Prabhu Deshpande, whose last stand at Ghod Khind — the pass later renamed Pavan Khind — held off Siddi Johar's pursuing troops so Shivaji could escape the Panhalgad blockade of 1660 and reach Vishalgad. Baji, in the standard account, gave his life to buy his master's escape, dying happy only once he heard the signal-guns confirming Shivaji had arrived safely.[^23] The second is Murar Baji Prabhu, commander of Purandar, who rallied his Mavalis against Diler Khan's Mughal siege in 1665, refused Diler Khan's offer of titles with the retort that he was "a true servant to Shivaji" and would sooner die than yield, and was shot dead with an arrow as he charged the Khan's elephant.[^24]

Keluskar narrates Murar Baji's death with his "usual fervour" — the Afghans recoiling from the swords of the infuriated Mavalis, the commander rushing the elephant "like a lion upon his prey."[^25] The fervour is real. But the *selection* is not neutral. The full elaboration of Baji Prabhu's story comes from Chitnis — and Chitnis was himself a CKP, employed at the Satara court at the very moment when Chitpavan brahmins were clinging to their authority in Pune and the CKPs were helping the Maratha rajas defend a fading royal heritage.[^26] A CKP chronicler at Satara was sure to highlight CKP heroes. The opposition between Chitpavan Pune and Maratha-CKP Satara, Laine notes, was a precursor of Phule's own movement.[^27]

So the pattern is the same one running through the mother-elevation, just aimed at the dead instead of the living mentors. Which martyrs get sung — Baji Prabhu, Murar Baji — is a function of the singer's caste. Whose mother becomes the engine of the legend, whose martyrs become its saints: in both cases the casting is a caste audit, and the patriotism on the surface had to "overcome or hide the fractious impulses of caste disputes" underneath.[^28]

## Implementation Workflow: How the Demotion Gets Played

The historian sits with two rival claims in front of him and a problem he cannot solve by force. Rajwade has written that the swaraj dream came from Dadaji. Ranade has built bhakti reform into the foundation. Both are Chitpavans; both have brahmins holding the credit. To answer them head-on is to be the marginal-caste writer picking a fight with the establishment — a fight he loses on status alone.

So he does not answer head-on. He picks up the mother instead. He writes the sentence about the sweet and loving word. He notes, almost in passing, that Shivaji did not meet Ramdas until 1672, the dates doing the demotion for him. He calls the Dadaji theory a heresy and lets the word sit. And he opens the whole book with the genealogy of a kshatriya king, handed to a prince who had just won that exact title back. Each move is gentle on its face. Together they hollow out the brahmin claim. And because the load-bearing piece is the mother, no reader can push back without seeming to insult her.

| Before — the dispute over the brahmin mentors | After — the unanswerable ode to the mother |
|---|---|
| Dadaji plants the dream of swaraj (Rajwade) | Dadaji "laboured hard to counteract" the dream; Jijabai is the real impulse |
| Ramdas the guru lights the spiritual fire | Ramdas met only in 1672, after the victories; influence may run the other way |
| Bhakti reform lays the religious ground (Ranade) | Pandharpur movement neither shaped the vision nor eased caste inequality |
| Credit sits with Chitpavan brahmins | Credit sits with the mother — and no Hindu can object |

Watch what the table costs the opponent. Every line on the left is a brahmin holding a piece of Shivaji. Every line on the right takes the piece back and parks it behind a figure that cannot be challenged. The writer never has to say "the brahmins are wrong." He only has to say "the mother is everything," and the rest follows.

## The Selective-Casting Failure (Diagnostic Signs)

You can spot this maneuver in any contested legend once you know the shape.

The first sign is an unchallengeable figure doing suspiciously heavy lifting. When a single source of a hero's greatness is also the one figure no one in the culture is permitted to question — the mother, the martyr, the saint, the founder — ask who benefits from putting the credit there. The unanswerability is the tell.

The second sign is a demotion that never gets argued. Keluskar never builds a case that Dadaji was unimportant; the importance simply evaporates the moment Jijabai is installed. When a rival is removed by displacement rather than by argument — crowded out, not refuted — the work is being done off the page, by the choice of who gets crowned.

The third sign is the caste fingerprint on the casting. When the heroes a writer elaborates all share his caste — Chitnis the CKP elaborating the CKP martyrs Baji Prabhu and Murar Baji — the selection is not a judgment about who was bravest. It is a judgment about whose bravery serves the singer. The legend's roster reads like a caste roster.

The failure to diagnose any of this is to read the sentiment as sentiment and stop there — to take the ode to the mother as nothing but love, the martyr-songs as nothing but patriotism, and to miss that the casting itself is the argument.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

The hard tension here must be kept open, not resolved.

On one side: Jijabai's formative role in Shivaji's life may have been entirely real. The vault's existing accounts of her — drawn from sources like Purandare — treat her as a genuine and decisive shaping force, the mother who held the household and the mission together while Shahji was away.[^29] Nothing in Laine requires us to say she was unimportant.

On the other side: that real importance is exactly what makes her strategically useful. Keluskar selects her *because* she is unchallengeable, and the selection demotes the brahmin mentors he wanted gone.[^30] A figure can be both genuinely formative and politically deployed. The deployment does not prove she was unimportant; the importance does not prove the deployment was innocent. Both are true at once, and Laine's reading lives precisely in that doubleness — he does not deny Jijabai mattered, he points out what Keluskar *does* with the fact that she mattered.[^31]

Open questions. Did Keluskar believe his own elevation, or know it was a move? (Probably both — sincerity and strategy are not exclusive.) Would the maneuver have worked outside the specific caste-politics of 1900s Maharashtra, or does it depend on that exact configuration of contested kshatriya status and Chitpavan dominance? And how far down does the selective casting go — if the mother and the martyrs are caste-selected, what about the villains, the betrayers, the minor saints? The vault does not resolve these. It holds them.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Stand inside the fight and you can feel the three writers pulling on the same body.

Keluskar reaches for Jijabai and pulls the credit toward the mother — and, underneath, toward the Marathas and the marginal castes whose hero he is defending. Rajwade reaches for Dadaji and pulls the credit toward the brahmin steward, lodging the swaraj dream in a brahmin's tutoring.[^32] Ranade reaches for the Pandharpur bhakti movement and pulls the credit toward brahmin-led religious reform as the ground of the whole national awakening.[^33] Three hands, one Shivaji, and each hand is also a caste.

The convergence first: all three agree Shivaji's greatness has a *source* outside himself that the historian's job is to name. None of them treats the king as self-made. They are arguing about the location of the engine, not its existence.

Then the tension sharpens into a caste-line. Rajwade and Ranade — and Tilak behind them — are Chitpavans, and their sources keep the credit in brahmin hands.[^34] Keluskar is a Saraswat allied with CKPs and Marathas, and his source moves the credit to the mother and, through her, to the non-brahmin coalition.[^35] The mother-versus-mentor fight is not really about Jijabai or Dadaji. It is about whether the brahmins or the Marathas own the founding.

And here is what the fight reveals: the question "who influenced Shivaji?" is unanswerable as history because it was never being asked as history. It was a proxy. Each writer's answer is a self-portrait of his caste's claim on the national hero. Keluskar's genius is to have found the one answer — the mother — that his opponents could not contest without breaking a taboo. He did not win the argument. He made the argument unwinnable for the other side.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

The plain point is this: the same move shows up wherever a story is being built to serve a claim, and seeing it in another domain sharpens what Keluskar is doing.

Start with [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/founding-myth-construction|Founding Myth Construction]]. A founding myth is never a neutral record; it is assembled to legitimate a present arrangement, and the assembly always involves choosing who gets to be the origin. Keluskar's elevation of Jijabai is founding-myth construction at the level of a single biography — he is deciding, for the Maratha claim, where the founding *began*. The handshake produces a sharp insight the history page alone does not generate: founding myths can be contested not by rewriting the facts but by relocating the credit to an unchallengeable figure. You do not have to deny that Dadaji existed. You only have to make the mother the source, and the founding quietly changes owners. The myth's real battleground is not "what happened" but "who counts as the beginning" — and the safest place to put the beginning is behind a figure the culture forbids you to question. That is a generalizable mechanism: every founding myth has an unattackable square on its board, and whoever reaches it first sets the lineage.

Now bring in [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/mother-warrior-synthesis|Mother-Warrior Synthesis]]. That page treats the mother-of-the-warrior as a recurring structural figure — the woman who forges the fighter, who stands behind the hero as the source of his fire. Keluskar is exploiting exactly that figure's cultural charge. But the handshake exposes a tension the synthesis page does not, on its own, surface: the mother-warrior bond is not only a psychological reality, it is a *rhetorical resource*. Because the figure is so charged, so unattackable, it can be picked up and used to do political work that has nothing to do with the bond itself. Keluskar weaponizes the reverence. The insight the pairing forces: the very sacredness that makes the mother-warrior figure powerful as experience is what makes her dangerous as argument — you cannot trust an appeal to the warrior's mother to be only about the mother, because the appeal is shielded from challenge by design. The more unchallengeable the figure, the more suspect any heavy reliance on her. Sanctity and manipulability are the same property seen from two sides.

A third, lighter handshake runs to [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/father-absence-and-the-daughters-search|Father Absence and the Search]]. Shahji, Shivaji's father, was largely absent — away in the Deccan service — which is part of what makes the mother-elevation historically plausible in the first place; the household was hers to run.[^36] The page on father-absence concerns the psychic search a missing father sets in motion. The structural echo here is at the level of the legend rather than the psyche: an absent father leaves an open slot at the origin of the story, and Keluskar fills it with the mother. The insight the connection yields: absence does not only shape a child, it shapes a *narrative* — the empty paternal slot is precisely the room a biographer needs to install the figure he wants. Where the father is missing, the mother's claim to be the source meets no rival, and the historian's strategic elevation becomes that much easier to make stick.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** The casting of a national legend is a caste audit. Whose mother becomes its engine, whose martyrs become its saints, whose mentors get quietly written out — every one of those choices is a position in a status fight, dressed as reverence or patriotism. Keluskar's ode to the mother is the cleanest specimen: the safest, most unattackable emotion in the culture, picked up and used as a blade against the brahmin claim on Shivaji. When you find an unchallengeable figure carrying the whole weight of a legend, you have found where the real fight is buried.

**Generative questions.**
- If the mother is the unanswerable square on the board, what is the equivalent square in a secular national myth — the figure who plays Jijabai's role in a story with no sacred mother to reach for?
- Keluskar's move worked because his opponents shared the taboo. What happens to the maneuver in a culture where the mother *can* be questioned — does the whole mechanism collapse, or just migrate to a new unchallengeable figure?
- If every martyr in the legend is caste-selected by his singer, can you reconstruct the caste-politics of a period purely from the roster of heroes its writers chose to elaborate — read the singers backward from the songs?

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/the-three-nationalist-visions|The Three Nationalist Visions]] — the Ranade/Tilak/Keluskar field this maneuver is played within
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/ranade-bhakti-as-the-ground-of-nationalism|Ranade — Bhakti as the Ground of Nationalism]] — the bhakti thesis Keluskar explicitly opposes by denying Pandharpur's influence
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/phule-the-low-caste-shivaji|Phule and the Low-Caste Shivaji]] — Keluskar's colleague; same caste sympathies, same CKP martyrs sung
